source_text:
Quis enim dubitet totum illud quod dicitur malum nihil esse aliud quam corruptionem ? possunt quidem aliis atque aliis uocabulis alia atque alia mala nominari, sed quod omnium rerum malum sit, in quibus mali aliquid animaduerti potest, corruptio est. sed corruptio peritae animae inperitia uocatur; corruptio prudentis inprudentia; corruptio iustae iniustitia; corruptio fortis ignauia; corruptio quietae atque tranquillae cupiditas uel metus uel tristitia uec iactantia; deinde in corpore animato corruptio sanitatis dolor et morbus; corruptio uirium lassitudo; corruptio quietis labor; deinde in ipso solo corpore corruptio pulchritudinis foeditas; corruptio rectitudinis prauitas; corruptio ordinis peruersitas; corruptio integritatis discissio aut fractura aut diminutio. longum est et difficile et harum rerum, quas commemoraui, et aliarum innumerabilium omnes corruptiones nominatim enuntiare, cum etiam multae, quae dicuntur in corpore, possint et in anima dici et innumerabilia sint, in quibus propria uocabula corruptio teneat. uerumtamen uidere iam facile est nihil nocere corruptionem, nisi quod labefacit naturalem statum, et ideo eam non esse naturam, sed contra naturam. quodsi non inuenitur in rebus malum nisi corruptio et corruptio non est natura, nulla utique natura malum est.
Sed si hoc forte intellegere non ualetis, illud adtendite, quod omne, quod corrumpitur, bono aliquo minuitur, quia si non corrumperetur, incorruptum esset; si uero etiam non posset omnino corrumpi, incorruptibile esset. necesse est autem, ut siue incorruptio siue incorruptibilitas bonum sit, si malum est corruptio. sed nunc de incorruptibili natura nulla quaesito est; de his agitur, quae possunt corrumpi quae dum non corrumpuntur, incorrupta dici possunt, incor- . ruptibilia non possunt. illud enim solum incorruptibile proprie dicitur, quod non tantum non corrumpitur, sed etiam nulla ex parte corrumpi potest. incorrupta ergo quaecumque sunt et tamen corrumpi possunt, cum corrumpi coeperint, eo ipso bono minuuntur, quo incorrupta erant, et magno quidem bono, quia magnum malum est corruptio; et quamdiu in eis augeri corruptio potest, tamdiu habent bonum, quo minuantur. quapropter naturae illae, quas in terra tenebrarum fuisse confingit. aut poterant corrumpi aut non poterant. si non poterant, incorruptibiles erant, quo bono superius nihil est. si poterant, aut corrumpebantur, aut non corrumpebantur; si non corrumpebantur, incorruptae erant, quod uidemus dici sine magna laude non posse; si autem corrumpebantur, minuebantur illo tam magno bono; si minuebantur quo bono, habebant bonum, quo minuerentur. quodsi habebant bonum, non erant naturae illae summum malum et omnis Manichaei fabula falsa est.
thought_title: Evil is corruption, not a nature
orientation: Augustine is now defining evil as corruption and applying this definition to Mani's land of darkness.
pass_a_gloss: Who [enim] would doubt [that] the whole [illud] which is called evil [to be] nothing other than corruption? [they] can indeed [by] other and other words other and other evils be named, but [that] which [of] all things [the] evil is, in which [of] evil something can be noticed, corruption is. but [the] corruption [of] a skilled soul unskillfulness is called; [the] corruption [of] a prudent [soul] imprudence; [the] corruption [of] a just [soul] injustice; [the] corruption [of] a brave [soul] cowardice; [the] corruption [of] a quiet and tranquil [soul] desire or fear or sadness or boastfulness; then in [an] animated body [the] corruption [of] health [is] pain and disease; [the] corruption [of] strength [is] weariness; [the] corruption [of] rest [is] labor; then in [the] bare body itself [the] corruption [of] beauty [is] ugliness; [the] corruption [of] straightness [is] crookedness; [the] corruption [of] order [is] perversity; [the] corruption [of] wholeness [is] splitting or breaking or diminution. long it is and difficult [both] [of] these things, which I have mentioned, and [of] other innumerable [things] all [the] corruptions by name to enumerate, since also many, which are said in [the] body, can also in [the] soul be said and innumerable they are, in which [their] own words corruption holds. nevertheless to see now easy it is [that] nothing harms corruption, except that it weakens [the] natural state, and therefore it not to be [a] nature, but against nature. [quodsi] if not is found in things evil except corruption and corruption not is [a] nature, no at all nature evil is. But if this by chance to understand you are not able, that attend [to], that everything, which is corrupted, [by] some good is diminished, because if not it were corrupted, uncorrupted it would be; if truly also not it could at all be corrupted, incorruptible it would be. necessary it is however, that whether incorruption whether incorruptibility [a] good is, if evil is corruption. but now about [an] incorruptible nature no question is; about these [things] it is dealt, which can be corrupted which while not they are corrupted, uncorrupted can be said, incorruptible not can. that [illud] alone incorruptible properly is said, which not only not is corrupted, but also [by] no part can be corrupted. uncorrupted therefore whatever [things] are and nevertheless can be corrupted, when to be corrupted they have begun, [by] that very good they are diminished, [by] which uncorrupted they were, and [by] a great indeed good, because [a] great evil is corruption; and as long as in them to increase corruption can, so long they have [the] good, [by] which they may be diminished. wherefore [those] natures, which in [the] land [of] darkness to have been he imagines, either could be corrupted or not could. if not they could, incorruptible they were, [by] which good higher nothing is. if they could, either they were being corrupted, or not they were being corrupted; if not they were being corrupted, uncorrupted they were, which we see to be said without great praise not to be able; if however they were being corrupted, they were diminished [by] that so great good; if they were diminished [by] which good, they had [the] good, [by] which they might be diminished. [quodsi] if they had [the] good, not were those natures [the] highest evil and [the] whole [of] Manichaeus [the] story false is.

choices.why: The glossary term for evil as loss of good; kept literal throughout.
Distinguishes 'not currently corrupted' from 'incorruptible' (cannot be corrupted), which is the key distinction Augustine draws.
Renders the stronger term for what cannot be corrupted at all.
Fixed glossary rendering for Mani's realm of evil.
Fixed glossary rendering for the greatest evil.
Captures Augustine's dismissive tone toward Mani's myth-making.

pass_b_english: Who would doubt that the whole of what is called evil is nothing other than corruption? Different evils can be named with different words, but the evil of all things in which any evil can be noticed is corruption. The corruption of a skilled soul is called unskillfulness; the corruption of a prudent soul, imprudence; of a just soul, injustice; of a brave soul, cowardice; of a quiet and tranquil soul, desire or fear or sadness or boasting. Then in a living body, the corruption of health is pain and disease; the corruption of strength is weariness; the corruption of rest is labor. Then in the body itself alone, the corruption of beauty is ugliness; the corruption of straightness is crookedness; the corruption of order is perversity; the corruption of wholeness is splitting or breaking or diminution. It would be long and difficult to name every corruption of the things I have mentioned and of countless others, since many that are said to be in the body can also be said to be in the soul, and there are countless cases where corruption holds its own proper names. But it is now easy to see that corruption harms nothing except by weakening the natural state, and therefore it is not a nature but against nature. And if nothing is found in things as evil except corruption, and corruption is not a nature, then no nature is evil.

But if perhaps you cannot understand this, attend to this point: everything that is corrupted is diminished in some good, because if it were not corrupted, it would be uncorrupted; and if it could not be corrupted at all, it would be incorruptible. It is necessary, however, that if corruption is an evil, then either being uncorrupted or being incorruptible is a good. But now there is no question about an incorruptible nature; we are dealing with things that can be corrupted, which while they are not corrupted can be called uncorrupted, but cannot be called incorruptible. For only that is properly called incorruptible which not only is not corrupted but also cannot be corrupted in any part. Therefore whatever things are uncorrupted and yet can be corrupted, when they begin to be corrupted, are diminished in that very good by which they were uncorrupted—and indeed in a great good, because corruption is a great evil. And as long as corruption can increase in them, so long do they have a good by which they may be diminished. Therefore those natures which he pretends existed in the land of darkness either could be corrupted or could not. If they could not, they were incorruptible, than which good nothing is higher. If they could, they were either being corrupted or not being corrupted. If they were not being corrupted, they were uncorrupted, which we see cannot be said without great praise. But if they were being corrupted, they were diminished in that so great a good; if they were diminished in a good, they had a good by which they might be diminished. And if they had a good, those natures were not the supreme evil, and the whole story of Mani is false.

last_rejected.why: Latin nouns 'incorruptio/incorruptibilitas' mean 'uncorruptedness/incorruptibility', not participles 'being uncorrupted/being incorruptible'.
last_rejected.fix: if either uncorruptedness or incorruptibility is a good
last_rejected.ruling: 'Being uncorrupted/incorruptible' accurately renders abstract nouns incorruptio/incorruptibilitas; gerund form is normal English.

last_rejected.quote: can be called uncorrupted, but cannot be called incorruptible
last_rejected.source_quote: incorrupta dici possunt, incorruptibilia non possunt
last_rejected.why: Latin uses adjectives as predicates, not passive periphrastics; 'incorrupta...incorruptibilia' are adjectives meaning 'uncorrupted...incorruptible'.
last_rejected.fix: are uncorrupted, but are not incorruptible
last_rejected.ruling: Adjectives incorrupta/incorruptibilia are correctly rendered 'uncorrupted/incorruptible'; no passive periphrastic in source.

last_rejected.quote: are diminished in that very good by which they were uncorrupted
last_rejected.source_quote: eo ipso bono minuuntur, quo incorrupta erant
last_rejected.why: Latin 'quo' is ablative of means/instrument, not 'by which' in a causal sense; better 'in that very good in which they were uncorrupted'.
last_rejected.fix: are diminished in that very good in which they were uncorrupted
last_rejected.ruling: 'By which' correctly renders ablative quo; 'in which' is a preference, not a correction.

last_rejected.quote: they were diminished in that so great a good
last_rejected.why: Latin 'illo...bono' is ablative; 'in that so great a good' is awkward and slightly misrepresents the construction as locative rather than ablative of respect.
last_rejected.fix: they were diminished by that so great good
last_rejected.ruling: 'In that so great a good' adequately renders ablative illo tam magno bono; slight awkwardness, not a major error.

problems.quote: if either being uncorrupted or being incorruptible is a good, then corruption is an evil
problems.source_quote: necesse est autem, ut siue incorruptio siue incorruptibilitas bonum sit, si malum est corruptio
problems.why: The conditional is reversed. Augustine argues that, given corruption is an evil, incorruption or incorruptibility must be a good. The English makes the goodness of incorruption the premise.
problems.fix: It is necessary, however, that if corruption is an evil, then either being uncorrupted or being incorruptible is a good.

edits.new: It is necessary, however, that if corruption is an evil, then either being uncorrupted or being incorruptible is a good.

fixed: modality: reversed conditional corrected to make corruption's evil the premise per 'si malum est corruptio'.
